newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan AIDS family accuses official of murder.
newsitem.headline: Japan AIDS family accuses official of murder.

text.p: The family of an AIDS victim urged prosecutors to bring murder charges against a former Japanese Health Ministry official on Wednesday.
The formal request for a prosecution, filed by a lawyer for the family, is the latest development in a decade-long scandal involving use of HIV-contaminated blood products on haemophiliacs.

The lawyer requested prosecutors in Osaka to act against Akihito Matsumura, who headed the ministry's Biologics and Antibiotics Division from 1984 to 1986. Matsumura, 55, resigned from the ministry in July and has now retired.
The victim's identity was not disclosed. A ministry official declined to comment on the matter and would not disclose Matsumura's whereabouts.

The complaint said Matsumura failed to order the recall of untreated blood products after official approval in 1985 of the production and sale of heated blood products, even though he knew unheated products could be contaminated with HIV, the virus that causes AIDS.
The family filed a similar complaint against the former president of pharmaceutical company Green Cross, which led to a police raid last month of the company's offices.

Wednesday's move against Matsumura is the first formal complaint against a public official and could open the way for investigations into the alleged role of the government in the scandal, in which some 400 haemophiliacs died after being given HIV-tainted products.
In a separate development, prosecutors said they had indicted the former head of a ministry AIDS research team who has been under arrest since last month.

Takeshi Abe was charged on Wednesday with professional negligence resulting in the death of a haemophiliac patient knowing that products he was treated with could have been tainted with the HIV virus.
Abe is believed to have influenced the team's conclusion in March 1984 to favour the use of unheated blood products, instead of using the safer heated products.

The Health Ministry, after maintaining for years it could not find documents, in February made public files from the 1983 study group Abe chaired which indicated health authorities were aware of the danger of HIV infection from unheated products.

In March, Japanese haemophiliacs accepted an out-of-court settlement in which the plaintiffs agreed to a one-time payment, putting an end to a seven-year legal battle against the state and five pharmaceutical firms.

Health Minister Naoto Kan became immensely popular because of his pivotal role in forcing his ministry to accept responsibility for the 1980s scandal, which infected some 1,800 haemophiliacs with HIV.
Recent Health Ministry figures show that there are 1,154 people with AIDS and 2,942 infected with the HIV virus in Japan, a nation of 125.6 million.
